meta.title: Hydraulic Systems: Pressure, Flow & Work
meta.interests: Agriculture, music, space, practical engineering and evidence-based technology

plan.title: Hydraulic Systems: Pressure, Flow & Work
plan.hook: A larger cylinder can lift more but move more slowly. Follow force, displaced volume and power to explain that trade without treating pressure and flow as interchangeable.
objectives: Relate pressure difference and effective area to cylinder force
Convert flow to piston speed using volume conservation
Identify load, valve and relief roles in a conceptual circuit
Compare two cylinder choices with a force, speed and power calculation
prerequisites: Basic multiplication and area units; these are paper models, not service procedures

sections.heading: Pressure is force per area
points: Model: friction and opposing pressure matter

sections.heading: Count the area on each side
points: Net force: subtract opposing chamber forces

sections.heading: Flow sets speed through displaced volume
points: Speed: actuator flow divided by area
Travel time: distance divided by steady speed

sections.heading: Trace the flow paths before blaming pressure
points: Evidence: pressure alone does not establish flow

sections.heading: Pressure times flow is power
points: Hydraulic power: pressure drop times flow
Efficiency: useful output over defined input

sections.heading: Capstone: choose a cylinder with evidence
points: Comparison: B meets the ideal limits
Margin: real losses can invalidate a boundary pass

sections.heading: Pressure is force per area
sections.body:
A hydraulic system transfers energy through a fluid. Pressure describes force per unit area; it is not a quantity of oil. One pascal, written Pa, is one newton per square metre. One megapascal, or MPa, is one million pascals.

In a static enclosed fluid, an applied pressure change is transmitted throughout the fluid. This does not remove pressure differences due to height or the losses that occur during flow. For a simplified piston with negligible opposing pressure and friction, force equals pressure difference multiplied by effective area.

At 10 MPa across a 20 cm² piston, convert area first: 20 cm² = 0.002 m². Force is 10,000,000 Pa × 0.002 m² = 20,000 N. Doubling area doubles force at the same pressure difference. It does not double energy for free: the larger piston needs more fluid for the same travel.

**Predict:** Does the pump outlet need high pressure when it supplies an easy open flow path? Not necessarily. The load and restrictions create the pressure requirement; pump behaviour and controls determine how the system responds.

**Try it:** Draw two pistons linked by a static fluid. Label equal pressure change but unequal forces. This course uses ideal calculations to build reasoning. Hydraulic equipment can retain dangerous energy; no lesson calls for opening lines or testing leaks by hand.
sections.visual: Connected pistons illustrate how the same static pressure change acts on different areas. Dimensions are schematic.

questions.q: Why can equal pressure produce unequal forces?
questions.answer: Force is pressure difference times area. A larger area experiences more force for the same difference.

questions.q: Why does a larger force not imply free energy?
questions.hint: The fluid volume required for travel changes.
questions.answer: The larger piston needs more volume per unit travel. Conservation of volume trades force against distance or speed in the ideal system.

sections.heading: Count the area on each side
sections.body:
A double-acting cylinder has a cap chamber and a rod chamber. The cap-side piston area is the full bore area. On the rod side, the rod occupies part of that area, leaving an annulus: bore area minus rod cross-sectional area.

Forces act in opposite directions. With cap pressure p-cap, rod pressure p-rod, bore area A-bore and rod-side effective area A-annulus, net extension force before friction is p-cap × A-bore − p-rod × A-annulus. Do not simply subtract pressures and multiply by full area when the two effective areas differ.

Suppose the bore area is 20 cm² and the rod area is 5 cm². Rod-side effective area is 15 cm². With 8 MPa driving one chamber and negligible pressure in the other, ideal extension force is 16,000 N; retraction force is 12,000 N. At equal inlet flow, retraction is faster because its driven area is smaller.

**Try it:** Add 1 MPa backpressure on the rod side during extension. Its opposing force is 1,000,000 × 0.0015 = 1,500 N, leaving 14,500 N before friction. State the chamber pressures as well as the areas. Real seals, geometry, load direction and efficiency can change the result.
sections.visual: The rod removes 5 cm² from a 20 cm² bore area. The cap and rod chambers therefore convert pressure and flow differently.
sections.diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 400"><rect x="1" y="1" width="798" height="398" rx="6" fill="#101a2a" stroke="#101a2a"/><text x="30" y="40" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="24" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">The rod changes the effective area</text><text x="30" y="70" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="15" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Equal pressure difference and inlet flow are compared separately.</text><rect x="80" y="135" width="600" height="130" rx="6" fill="#243e54" stroke="#a8b9d0"/><rect x="330" y="138" width="30" height="124" rx="6" fill="#f8bf70" stroke="#f8bf70"/><rect x="360" y="182" width="375" height="38" rx="6" fill="#a8b9d0" stroke="#a8b9d0"/><line x1="145" y1="190" x2="305" y2="190" stroke="#69d9d0" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M 297.10 194.31 L 305 190 L 297.10 185.69" fill="none" stroke="#69d9d0" stroke-width="3"/><text x="95" y="118" fill="#69d9d0" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Cap side: full bore</text><text x="425" y="118" fill="#f8bf70" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Rod side: annular area</text><text x="100" y="305" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Bore area: 20 cm²</text><text x="425" y="305" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Rod area: 5 cm²</text><text x="425" y="334" fill="#f8bf70" font-size="18" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Net rod-side area: 15 cm²</text><text x="30" y="377" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Conceptual model; assumptions and units are explained in the lesson.</text></svg>

questions.q: Why is ideal retraction force lower at equal driving pressure?
questions.hint: The rod occupies part of one face.
questions.answer: The rod-side effective area is smaller. Equal pressure acting across it produces less force.

questions.q: What is extension force with 8 MPa cap pressure and 1 MPa rod pressure in the example?
questions.answer: 16,000 N from the cap minus 1,500 N from the rod side gives 14,500 N before friction.

sections.heading: Flow sets speed through displaced volume
sections.body:
Flow rate is volume per time. A litre per minute is a useful equipment unit, but piston calculations become clearer in cubic metres per second. One litre is 0.001 m³; one minute is 60 seconds.

For an incompressible fluid, a piston moving a distance sweeps volume equal to its effective area times travel. Dividing by time gives flow equals area times speed. Therefore speed equals flow divided by area, when leakage and fluid compression are negligible.

At 12 L/min, flow is 12 × 0.001 / 60 = 0.0002 m³/s. A 20 cm² area is 0.002 m². Speed is 0.0002 / 0.002 = 0.10 m/s. A 0.50 m stroke takes 0.50 / 0.10 = 5 s under a constant-speed assumption. Doubling area at the same flow halves speed.

The inlet and outlet flow rates of a double-acting cylinder can differ because the two swept volumes differ. That matters when considering return-path restrictions. A constant pump flow also does not guarantee all flow reaches the cylinder if another path is open.

**Try it:** Repeat the example with 6 L/min. Speed becomes 0.05 m/s and stroke time 10 s. Explain which assumption would fail if half the supply bypassed the actuator.
sections.visual: Two piston areas receive the same ideal flow. The larger area has half the speed; the horizontal bars compare speeds on one scale.
sections.diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 400"><rect x="1" y="1" width="798" height="398" rx="6" fill="#101a2a" stroke="#101a2a"/><text x="30" y="40" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="24" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Volume links flow to speed</text><text x="30" y="70" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="15" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Same inlet flow, different ideal piston areas.</text><text x="195" y="167" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">Area 20 cm²</text><rect x="210" y="145" width="475" height="30" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#33445e"/><rect x="210" y="145" width="395.83333333333337" height="30" rx="6" fill="#69d9d0" stroke="#69d9d0"/><text x="697" y="167" fill="#69d9d0" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">0.1 m/s</text><text x="195" y="267" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">Area 40 cm²</text><rect x="210" y="245" width="475" height="30" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#33445e"/><rect x="210" y="245" width="197.91666666666669" height="30" rx="6" fill="#f8bf70" stroke="#f8bf70"/><text x="697" y="267" fill="#f8bf70" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">0.05 m/s</text><text x="30" y="377" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">12 L/min = 0.0002 m³/s. Speed = flow / effective area; larger area moves slower.</text></svg>

questions.q: Why does doubling area halve speed at fixed flow?
questions.hint: Consider the volume needed for one centimetre of travel.
questions.answer: Twice the area needs twice the volume per unit travel. The same delivered flow therefore moves it at half the speed.

questions.q: What if half of the 12 L/min bypasses the cylinder?
questions.hint: Use actuator flow rather than pump flow.
questions.answer: Only 6 L/min enters the 20 cm² chamber, so ideal speed falls to 0.05 m/s.

sections.heading: Trace the flow paths before blaming pressure
sections.body:
A pump supplies flow; a directional valve selects paths; an actuator converts fluid power into motion. A reservoir receives returning fluid. A relief valve can provide a pressure-limiting path when its opening condition is reached. This is a role map, not a complete machine circuit.

If a cylinder is stalled against a load, continued pump flow must go somewhere, be reduced by pump controls, or cause pressure to rise toward a limit. In a simple fixed-flow teaching circuit with a relief path, flow can return to tank through relief while the cylinder remains still. High indicated pressure then coexists with no useful piston motion.

A throttle restriction can control flow but creates a pressure drop and dissipates energy. The pressure at a pump, valve and cylinder need not match during flow. A single pressure reading does not tell you actuator flow, load force or where losses occur.

**Predict:** Does a stationary cylinder at high pressure prove that the pump has failed? No. A heavy load, blocked path, relief condition or mechanical constraint could produce that observation.

**Try it:** On the conceptual drawing, trace a moving-actuator path and a stalled-with-relief path. List the pressure, motion and flow evidence that would distinguish them. Actual diagnostic testing must follow the equipment’s service procedure and rated instrumentation; this exercise requires no hardware.
sections.visual: The normal route and a relief-to-tank branch are shown separately. Real circuits require additional components and equipment-specific documentation.

questions.q: How can high pressure coexist with no cylinder movement?
questions.hint: Where can the supplied flow go?
questions.answer: The cylinder may be stalled while flow bypasses through a relief path, or pump controls may reduce flow. Pressure alone does not show useful motion.

questions.q: Why do we need more than one pressure reading to understand a loss?
questions.answer: The pressure difference across a restriction, together with its flow, identifies dissipated hydraulic power; one absolute reading cannot do that.

sections.heading: Pressure times flow is power
sections.body:
Force alone does not describe how fast a hydraulic system does work. Mechanical power is force times speed. For ideal fluid transfer, hydraulic power is pressure difference times volumetric flow. Pascals times cubic metres per second produce watts.

At 10 MPa and 12 L/min, hydraulic power is 10,000,000 × 0.0002 = 2,000 W. If 2 MPa is lost across a throttle at that same flow, the throttle dissipates 2,000,000 × 0.0002 = 400 W. Only 8 MPa remains across an ideal actuator returning to negligible pressure: 1,600 W.

For the 20 cm² actuator, force is 16,000 N and speed 0.10 m/s. Their product is also 1,600 W, so the two calculation paths agree. This cross-check catches unit errors. Actual shaft input exceeds hydraulic output because pumps and drives are imperfect; actuator output can also be reduced by leakage and friction.

Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power for a clearly stated boundary. If measured shaft input is 2,500 W and useful actuator output is 1,600 W, whole-boundary efficiency is 64%.

**Try it:** Separate pump losses from throttle losses in a ledger. Explain why a stalled actuator can heat the oil even though its mechanical output power is zero.
sections.visual: A shared flow makes pressure-drop power accounting possible. The 2,000 W input splits into 1,600 W ideal actuator output and 400 W throttle heat.

questions.q: What hydraulic power crosses 8 MPa at 12 L/min?
questions.hint: Convert litres per minute to cubic metres per second.

questions.q: Why can a stalled system still generate heat?
questions.hint: Zero motion means zero useful actuator power, not necessarily zero input.
questions.answer: Flow dissipated across relief or restrictions converts input power to heat while the stationary actuator does no mechanical work.

sections.heading: Capstone: choose a cylinder with evidence
sections.body:
A fictional mechanism needs at least 25,000 N while extending at 0.05 m/s or faster. Compare cylinder A with bore area 20 cm² and cylinder B with 40 cm². Both receive 12 L/min at an 8 MPa cap-to-return pressure difference. Ignore friction, leakage, acceleration and return backpressure for this first comparison.

**Your task:** Calculate force, speed and ideal power for each. Decide which meets both requirements. State two reasons the decision would need further verification on real equipment.

**Worked solution:** Flow is 0.0002 m³/s. A produces 8,000,000 × 0.002 = 16,000 N at 0.0002 / 0.002 = 0.10 m/s. B produces 32,000 N at 0.05 m/s. Both have 1,600 W ideal output. B meets the stated force and speed limits in the model; A fails the force requirement. B has no speed margin, so actual losses or lower delivered flow could invalidate the choice.

**Check your work:** Include converted areas, actuator flow, pressure difference, both requirement comparisons and the energy cross-check. Record load variation and stroke geometry as further questions. Equal power does not make the two cylinders interchangeable. This paper selection is not a component approval: mounts, stability, ratings and the complete circuit remain outside the model.
sections.visual: The comparison preserves identical ideal input conditions. Cylinder B gains force by giving up speed, and its speed result sits exactly at the requirement.

questions.q: Which cylinder meets the stated ideal requirements?
questions.hint: Check both limits, not force alone.
questions.answer: B produces 32,000 N at 0.05 m/s and meets both model limits. A reaches 0.10 m/s but only 16,000 N.

questions.q: Why is B’s speed result a fragile pass?
questions.hint: Compare the answer with the minimum.
questions.answer: Its ideal 0.05 m/s equals the minimum. Reduced delivered flow, leakage or other real effects could leave it below the requirement.

questions.q: At 5 MPa across 20 cm², what is ideal force?
What establishes a pressure requirement during operation?
choices: The load and restrictions opposing flow
The paint colour of the pump
questions.explain: Pressure develops in response to load and restrictions, within pump and control limits.

questions.q: Which statement correctly applies Pascal’s principle?
choices: Pressure is identical at every height and flow condition
Every piston travels the same distance
An applied static pressure change is transmitted through an enclosed fluid
questions.explain: The principle concerns pressure changes in enclosed static fluid; it is not a guarantee of equal forces or energy multiplication.

questions.q: A bore area is 30 cm² and rod area 8 cm². What is rod-side effective area?
Why is multiplying net pressure by full bore area generally wrong for this cylinder?
choices: Pressure cannot act on a rod chamber
The rod area is always zero
Opposing pressures act on different effective areas
questions.explain: Each chamber force needs its own pressure and effective area before subtraction.

questions.q: At equal inlet flow, which stroke is faster in this ideal example?
choices: Retraction through the smaller effective area
Extension because its area is bigger
Neither can move unless both chambers are pressurized equally
questions.explain: Speed equals inlet flow divided by driven area, so the smaller annular area moves faster.

questions.q: At 6 L/min into 20 cm², what is ideal speed?
questions.explain: 6 L/min = 0.0001 m³/s; divide by 0.002 m² to obtain 0.05 m/s.

questions.q: At 0.10 m/s, how long is a 0.50 m steady stroke?
Why can inlet and return flows differ on a moving double-acting cylinder?
choices: Both sides always have full bore area
The two sides have unequal swept areas
Fluid must vanish inside the piston
The flow meter changes pressure units
questions.explain: The common piston speed multiplies different chamber areas, producing different volumetric flows.

questions.q: In the teaching circuit, where can fixed pump flow go after the cylinder stalls?
choices: Through an open relief path to the reservoir
It must become useful lifting work
questions.explain: The relief path can carry flow while pressure remains high and the actuator is stationary.

questions.q: Which quantity is missing if you know only a throttle’s pressure drop?
questions.explain: Dissipated hydraulic power is pressure drop times flow; pressure drop alone is insufficient.

questions.q: What does a directional valve primarily determine?
choices: The fluid’s mass without any motion
questions.explain: Valve connections establish flow routes; loads, metering, supply and controls affect actual pressure and speed.

questions.q: What power is dissipated across 2 MPa at 12 L/min?
Useful output is 1,600 W and shaft input 2,500 W. What is efficiency?
questions.explain: 1,600 / 2,500 = 0.64. Input and output must describe the same boundary and interval.

questions.q: Which independent calculation should match ideal actuator hydraulic power?
questions.explain: Force × speed equals mechanical power, matching pressure difference × flow in the ideal actuator.

questions.q: What is cylinder B’s ideal extension force?
Why do A and B have equal ideal output power?
choices: Both receive the same pressure difference and flow
questions.explain: Equal pressure difference × flow gives equal ideal power, with a force-speed trade.

questions.q: What would most directly challenge B’s speed pass?
choices: A change in the diagram colour
questions.explain: Speed depends on actual delivered flow divided by effective area; B has no speed margin.

sections.title: Pressure is force per area
bullets: Model: friction and opposing pressure matter
sections.notes: Force is pressure difference times area. A larger area experiences more force for the same difference. The larger piston needs more volume per unit travel. Conservation of volume trades force against distance or speed in the ideal system.
sections.visual: Connected pistons illustrate how the same static pressure change acts on different areas. Dimensions are schematic.

sections.title: Count the area on each side
bullets: Net force: subtract opposing chamber forces
sections.notes: The rod-side effective area is smaller. Equal pressure acting across it produces less force. 16,000 N from the cap minus 1,500 N from the rod side gives 14,500 N before friction.
sections.visual: The rod removes 5 cm² from a 20 cm² bore area. The cap and rod chambers therefore convert pressure and flow differently.

sections.title: Flow sets speed through displaced volume
bullets: Speed: actuator flow divided by area
Travel time: distance divided by steady speed
sections.notes: Twice the area needs twice the volume per unit travel. The same delivered flow therefore moves it at half the speed. Only 6 L/min enters the 20 cm² chamber, so ideal speed falls to 0.05 m/s.
sections.visual: Two piston areas receive the same ideal flow. The larger area has half the speed; the horizontal bars compare speeds on one scale.

sections.title: Trace the flow paths before blaming pressure
bullets: Evidence: pressure alone does not establish flow
sections.notes: The cylinder may be stalled while flow bypasses through a relief path, or pump controls may reduce flow. Pressure alone does not show useful motion. The pressure difference across a restriction, together with its flow, identifies dissipated hydraulic power; one absolute reading cannot do that.
sections.visual: The normal route and a relief-to-tank branch are shown separately. Real circuits require additional components and equipment-specific documentation.

sections.title: Pressure times flow is power
bullets: Hydraulic power: pressure drop times flow
Efficiency: useful output over defined input
sections.notes: 8,000,000 Pa × 0.0002 m³/s = 1,600 W. Flow dissipated across relief or restrictions converts input power to heat while the stationary actuator does no mechanical work.
sections.visual: A shared flow makes pressure-drop power accounting possible. The 2,000 W input splits into 1,600 W ideal actuator output and 400 W throttle heat.

sections.title: Capstone: choose a cylinder with evidence
bullets: Comparison: B meets the ideal limits
Margin: real losses can invalidate a boundary pass
sections.notes: B produces 32,000 N at 0.05 m/s and meets both model limits. A reaches 0.10 m/s but only 16,000 N. Its ideal 0.05 m/s equals the minimum. Reduced delivered flow, leakage or other real effects could leave it below the requirement.
sections.visual: The comparison preserves identical ideal input conditions. Cylinder B gains force by giving up speed, and its speed result sits exactly at the requirement.

turns.line: What hydraulic power crosses 8 MPa at 12 L/min?

turns.line: Why can a stalled system still generate heat?
